## What each one does

**Merge** creates a new commit that ties two branch histories together. Both branches' commits stay exactly as they were, and a merge commit sits on top with two parents.

```
main:     A---B---C-------M
                       \  /
feature:                D---E
```

**Rebase** replays your branch's commits one by one onto a new base, rewriting them as new commits with new hashes. No merge commit, no branching — just a straight line.

```
before:   A---B---C          (main)
                \
                 D---E        (feature)

after:    A---B---C---D'---E' (feature, rebased)
```

## The actual difference

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves what really happened, branches and all | Rewrites history into a straight line |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed (new commits replace old) |
| Safety on shared branches | Safe — never rewrites existing commits | Unsafe if others already pulled the old commits |
| Result | Extra merge commit, messier graph | Clean, linear graph |

## When to reach for each

- **Rebase your own local/feature branch** before opening a PR, to clean up messy "wip" commits and make the diff easy to review. Safe because nobody else depends on those commit hashes yet.
- **Merge when integrating a shared/team branch into main**, or once a branch is public and others have based work on it. Rewriting shared history breaks everyone else's clone.
- **Never rebase a branch other people are actively pulling from** — it forces everyone to force-pull or fix broken histories.

Rule of thumb: rebase to clean up before sharing, merge to combine after sharing.
